prompt: What three factors does the passage give for creating the right atmosphere for mental development?

options.text: Quietness, separation and keeping wise company
Research, meditation and prayer
Salvation, the fear of God and meekness
Singing, meditation and worship

explanation: Three headings in the chapter, summarised at its close. Creating a conducive atmosphere for development means creating an atmosphere conducive for divine inspiration.

why.a: Correct. Quietness, separation and wise company are the three, each with its own section.
why.b: Wrong. Research, meditation, consultants and prayer are the FOUR ways to exercise the mind in Chapter 8.
why.c: Wrong. Those are three of the four requirements for divine wisdom in Chapter 4.
why.d: Wrong. Singing and meditation are the two ways to generate inspiration in Chapter 6.

prompt: How does the passage say the Bible describes quietness?

options.text: As a virtue of great price, which carries valuable treasures
As the mark of a disciplined man
As the beginning of wisdom
As a discipline that must be learned in youth

explanation: 1 Peter 3:4 speaks of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. The reason quietness is valuable is that it facilitates inspiration.

why.a: Correct. Of great price is the phrase from the verse, and the author reads it as carrying valuable treasures.
why.b: Wrong. Discipline is not the framing used.
why.c: Wrong. The beginning of wisdom is the FEAR OF THE LORD, from Proverbs 9:10 in Chapter 4.
why.d: Wrong. Age is never mentioned here, and Chapter 6 says inspiration has nothing to do with age.

prompt: In the account of Elijah at the cave, where was God not found?

options.text: In the earthquake, the fire and the strong wind
In the ravens that fed him
In the fire that fell on Carmel
In the chariot that took him up

explanation: Three dramatic phenomena, and God in none of them. It was in the midst of the still small voice that a new chapter was opened up to him, which is why the story sits under QUIETNESS.

why.a: Correct. Earthquake, fire and strong wind are the three named, and the passage says God was not there.
why.b: Wrong. The ravens belong to a different part of Elijah's story and are not in this book.
why.c: Wrong. Carmel is not mentioned, and the fire here is at the cave.
why.d: Wrong. The chariot is not part of this account.

prompt: What does the passage say Elijah was doing when the virtue of quietness paid off for him?

options.text: He was out on a suicide mission and wanted to die, lying tired by the mouth of a cave
He was fasting for forty days
He was interceding for the nation
He was training his successor

explanation: The detail is stark and is the point: quietness worked for him at his lowest, in the midst of his despair, and God used the moment to demonstrate a great drama on how to encounter inspiration.

why.a: Correct. At the point of giving up, wanting to die, laid tired by the mouth of a cave.
why.b: Wrong. Forty days of fasting appears in this book only in Chapter 9, of a man who fasted over a supposed curse without thinking for a second.
why.d: Wrong. Elisha appears separately, in Chapter 6 with the minstrel.

prompt: Why does the passage say the practice of quietness is a requirement for mental development?

options.text: Because the voice of the Lord always comes down in a still voice, so you have to be extra still
Because noise damages the memory over time
Because the mind can only hold one thought at a time
Because rest restores the brain's capacity

explanation: Isaiah 30:21 is cited, that you will hear a voice BEHIND you, which the author uses to argue you must be extra still to catch it. Quietness matters because it facilitates inspiration.

why.a: Correct. The stillness of the voice is what requires stillness in the hearer.
why.b: Wrong. No claim about memory damage is made.
why.c: Wrong. Single-tasking is not an idea this book uses.
why.d: Wrong. Rest is not discussed; the book's rest is Solomon's rest on every side, which is peace rather than sleep.

prompt: Which scripture is the text for separation?

options.text: Proverbs 18:1
Proverbs 13:20
1 Thessalonians 4:11
1 Peter 3:4

explanation: Proverbs 18:1: 'Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom.' The condition is DESIRE, which the author underlines at the end of the section.

why.a: Correct. Proverbs 18:1 is the separation verse.
why.b: Wrong. Proverbs 13:20 is 'He that walketh with wise men shall be wise', the text for KEEPING WISE COMPANY.
why.c: Wrong. 1 Thessalonians 4:11 on studying to be quiet belongs to the quietness section, and is used again in Chapter 9.
why.d: Wrong. 1 Peter 3:4 is the meek and quiet spirit of great price, also from quietness.

prompt: Where did the author travel when he had a big problem and needed to be alone?

options.text: Accra, Ghana
Tulsa, Oklahoma
Benin
London

explanation: Accra, where he told the missionaries no telephone calls, no personal contacts, no one comes around, and that he was not there for the church and would not preach or teach anywhere.

why.a: Correct. Accra, Ghana is where he went to be alone.
why.b: Wrong. Tulsa, Oklahoma is where he visited Kenneth E. Hagin, in Chapter 2.
why.c: Wrong. Benin is where Archbishop Benson Idahosa showed him the building that had lost relevance, in Chapter 10.
why.d: Wrong. London is where the owner of that Benin building lived, not somewhere the author went.

prompt: What happened at the seashore in Accra, according to the passage?

options.text: After walking about two kilometres he sat down, picked his pen alone under a little canopy, and had showers from heaven
He fasted three days and then received an answer
He met a stranger who gave him counsel
He read through an entire book in one sitting

explanation: The two kilometres and the little canopy are the concrete details. By the time he got back to Nigeria he was fully armed with what to do to deal with the problem.

why.a: Correct. Two kilometres, the pen, the canopy and showers from heaven.
why.b: Wrong, and it is a near miss, because a 3-day trip appears in the very next paragraph. That is the SEPARATE prosperity story, where the heavens came down on the third day.
why.c: Wrong. The whole point of the trip was that no one came around.
why.d: Wrong. He armed himself with materials on the OTHER trip; here he wrote.

prompt: On the trip taken to establish his stand on prosperity, when did the heavens come down, and what date is attached?

options.text: On the third day of a 3-day trip, dated May 1981
On the first morning, dated 1974
On the third day, dated May 1974
After a week of separation, dated 1981

explanation: A 3-day trip, the heavens coming down on the third day, and what he laid hold of that day, May 1981, is still with him as fresh as the day it was delivered.

why.a: Correct. Third day of three, May 1981.
why.b: Wrong. 1974 is when Norman Vincent Pearle taught him the power of positive thinking, in Chapter 2.
why.c: Wrong. The day is right but the year belongs to the Pearle story.
why.d: Wrong. The trip was three days, not a week.

prompt: What does the passage say about Isaac sowing in the land in Genesis 26:12?

options.text: It was NOT that he gave offering; he sowed practical seeds and reaped a bumper harvest because he knew what to do
It means he gave a tithe of everything he had
It means he invested in the trade of the region
It means he taught the people to farm

explanation: The correction is explicit and is aimed at a common preaching reading. Isaac's advantage came from separation: he went out to meditate, per Genesis 24:63, and got extraordinary insights on how to make things work in spite of famine.

why.a: Correct. The passage denies the offering reading and insists on literal seeds sown with insight.
why.b: Wrong. This is precisely the interpretation the sentence rules out.
why.d: Wrong. Teaching others is not part of Isaac's story here.

prompt: What did Bill Gates reply when his mother found him and asked what he was doing?

options.text: "I am thinking! Don't you think!"
"I am working on something important"
"I am reading, please leave me"
"I am building something you will see one day"

explanation: She had called out 'Bill! Bill! Where are you?' with no sound and no response. The author calls him the computer giant and says we can see the results of those times of separation today.

why.a: Correct. This is the reply as printed, including the retort.
why.b: Wrong. Working is not the word, and thinking is the point of the whole anecdote.
why.c: Wrong. Reading is not what he was doing; the story is about thinking in solitude.
why.d: Wrong. Nothing about building is said.

prompt: What does the passage say every author will agree about solid material?

options.text: That every solid material he gets is delivered in solitary corners
That it comes only after long revision
That it comes from wide reading rather than original thought
That it arrives unbidden and cannot be sought

explanation: It is the justification for separation, which entails getting out of the crowd and multitude and getting yourself to a corner alone.

why.a: Correct. Solitary corners is the phrase, and it is attributed to every author's experience.
why.b: Wrong. Revision is never discussed in this book.
why.c: Wrong. Wide reading is urged in Chapters 2 and 8, but the claim here is about solitude.
why.d: Wrong. The chapter gives methods for seeking it, so it is not unbidden.

prompt: Which scripture is the text for keeping wise company?

options.text: Proverbs 13:20
Proverbs 11:14
Proverbs 18:1
Proverbs 27:17

explanation: Proverbs 13:20: 'He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.' Both halves matter, the promise and the warning.

why.a: Correct. Proverbs 13:20 heads the wise company section.
why.b: Wrong. Proverbs 11:14 on the multitude of counsellors belongs to Chapter 8, under consultants.
why.c: Wrong. Proverbs 18:1 is the separation verse from earlier in this same chapter.
why.d: Wrong. Proverbs 27:17 on iron sharpening iron is used in Chapter 8, under research.

prompt: How does the passage say you can keep wise company without the person being present?

options.text: Through materials like books and tapes, making authors and preachers your friends in absentia
By writing letters and awaiting their replies
By joining a church where they once ministered
By imagining conversations with them

explanation: The phrase is friends in absentia. Every book you read is the author's thoughts in print, so reading is keeping company with him, and in no time you will start thinking the same way.

why.a: Correct. Books and tapes, and friends in absentia is the author's own phrase.
why.b: Wrong, and it is a near miss, because Chapter 8 does mention writing a letter to ask a question. That is under CONSULTANTS, a different section.
why.c: Wrong. Church affiliation is not proposed.
why.d: Wrong. Imagination has its own chapter and is not applied this way.

prompt: According to the saying quoted, what two things will change who you are in five years?

options.text: The books you read and the people with whom you walk
The habits you keep and the goals you set
The prayers you pray and the sacrifices you make
The risks you take and the failures you survive

explanation: 'You'll remain the same way you are today in five years, except for two things: the books you read and the people with whom you walk.' The two map exactly onto this chapter's third factor and Chapter 8's research.

why.a: Correct. Books and people are the two named, which is why the saying sits under wise company.
why.b: Wrong. Habits and goals are not the book's vocabulary.
why.c: Wrong. Prayer and sacrifice are not the two named here.
why.d: Wrong. Risk and failure belong to Chapter 9's material on rising after a fall.

prompt: What test does the passage give for determining who to associate with?

options.text: Find out whether what the person is saying is profiting him or her or not
Find out whether they share your convictions
Find out how long they have walked with God
Find out whether they are willing to correct you

explanation: A results test rather than a doctrinal one. It matches Chapter 8's rule for consultants, that they are men who have results in their areas of specialization, and that you should look for those with testimonies.

why.a: Correct. Whether it is profiting them is the test, which is a test of results.
why.b: Wrong. Agreement is not the criterion offered.
why.c: Wrong. Longevity in ministry is admired in Chapter 8, but it is not this test.
why.d: Wrong. Willingness to correct is never mentioned.

prompt: How does the Amplified Version of Job 32:8 read, as quoted in the book?

options.text: "But there is [a vital force] a spirit [of intelligence] in man, and the breath of the Almighty gives men understanding"
"The spirit of a man is the candle of the LORD"
"The inspiration of the Almighty is the light of understanding"
"There is a wisdom in man that no teaching can supply"

explanation: The bracketed insertions are what make it quotable: a vital force, and a spirit of intelligence. It is quoted twice, in Chapter 7 and again in Chapter 10.

why.a: Correct. This is the Amplified rendering as printed, brackets and all.
why.b: Wrong. That is a real Proverbs verse that this book does not quote.
why.c: Wrong. A plausible paraphrase but not the Amplified text given.
why.d: Wrong. An invented line in the right register.

prompt: What does the passage say about outstanding insight and God's input?

options.text: Every outstanding insight has God's input, and God's input is contacted through inspiration
God's input is given only in answer to prayer
God's input can be recognised by the peace it brings
God's input is confirmed through the counsel of others

explanation: It follows Jeremiah 9:23-24, that the one who glories should glory in knowing God. Inspiration is the contact point, which is why quietness matters so much.

why.a: Correct. Both halves are stated, and inspiration is named as the channel.
why.b: Wrong. Prayer is one of four ways to exercise the mind in Chapter 8, not the sole channel for God's input.
why.c: Wrong. Peace is a product of wisdom, not a test of input.
why.d: Wrong. Counsel is valued in Chapter 8, but not as a confirmation mechanism for insight.

prompt: Fill the blank: "Every book you read is the author's {{1}} in print."
explanation: Thoughts, which is what makes reading a way of keeping company: you are sharing his thoughts and rubbing minds with him, and in no time you start thinking the same way.

prompt: The passage teaches that a person can live in the midst of noise and still make the most of the mind.

options.text: True
False

explanation: False. 'You can't live in the midst of noise and make the most of this treasure called the mind.' The chapter closes by telling you to switch off the noise and row in your environment.

why.true: Wrong. It contradicts a flat statement in the chapter.
why.false: Correct. Noise and mental excellence are treated as incompatible, which is why quietness and separation are two of the three factors.

prompt: What comparison opens the chapter on creating the right atmosphere?

options.text: That every living thing needs a conducive atmosphere, and even plants need the right condition to grow
That a fire needs fuel and air to keep burning
That a seed must die before it can bear fruit
That a river runs clean only while it is moving

explanation: The plant comparison sets up the chapter: if you want the best results or harvest, conditions matter, and the same holds for mental development.

why.a: Correct. Plants and the right conditions for growth open the chapter.
why.b: Wrong. Fire imagery appears only in the closing prophecies of Chapter 11.
why.c: Wrong. Seed language IS used in Chapter 8, of the gift as a seed to be nurtured, but not here.
why.d: Wrong. Rivers appear only inside the Job 28 and Isaiah 43 quotations.
